text: The duplicate-rate score on the CMDB Health Dashboard doesn't appear from nowhere -- it traces back to specific, repeatable causes. This lesson covers the two most common ones, the built-in tooling that surfaces duplicates already sitting in your CMDB, and the real fix, which is not simply deleting the extra record.

An Identification Rule that's too loose or outright misconfigured lets two records describing the same real asset get created side by side instead of being recognized as one, which the previous lesson covered in detail. The other common cause is a timing and matching gap: a CI gets entered manually, often during a project before Discovery has ever scanned that environment, and later Discovery finds the same physical or virtual asset but fails to correctly match it to the existing record, creating a second one instead of updating the first. Both causes trace back to the same underlying weakness in identification logic.

For duplicates that already exist, ServiceNow's built-in duplicate-detection reporting compares records using the same kind of attributes an Identification Rule would use -- matching serial numbers, matching IP addresses, near-identical hostnames -- and flags pairs worth a human review. This is deliberately a review step, not an automatic delete; a tool can surface strong candidates, but a person still confirms two flagged records genuinely are the same asset before anything gets consolidated.

Once a pair is confirmed, the correct action is to merge the two records into one surviving CI, never to simply delete the extra one. By the time a CI has been in the CMDB even a few weeks, it's likely accumulated real relationships to other CIs, Incident and Change records logged against it, and possibly Business Service mappings depending on it. Deleting a duplicate deletes all of that silently -- every incident ever logged against it loses its link, every relationship pointing at it becomes orphaned, with no error raised anywhere. A proper merge instead re-points that history onto the single record that survives.

Put together, the real-world cleanup pattern is: run duplicate detection, review the flagged pairs for genuine matches, merge confirmed duplicates onto one surviving record, and then go fix the Identification Rule that let the duplication happen in the first place -- otherwise the same problem just repeats on the next Discovery run. Next up: the governance and ownership piece that keeps a CMDB accurate for good, not just for one cleanup sprint.
